stem: A hospital is implementing an Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health (AIM) patient safety bundle for obstetric hemorrhage. Which implementation approach best reflects the purpose of the bundle?

options.A: Use the bundle’s evidence-informed actionable practices, adapt implementation to the facility’s resources and setting, and standardize the agreed process within the institution while preserving patient-specific clinical judgment.
options.B: Treat every bundle element as an inflexible national order set that must be applied identically in every facility and to every patient.
options.C: Use the bundle only for patients already known to be high risk because patient safety bundles are not intended to improve general systems of maternal care.
options.D: Replace ongoing clinical assessment and individualized treatment decisions with the bundle checklist once implementation begins.

rationale: A is correct. Current AIM guidance defines patient safety bundles as collections of evidence-informed best practices developed by multidisciplinary experts to improve processes of care and outcomes for clinically specific conditions in pregnant and postpartum patients. Bundles contain actionable steps that can be adapted to different facilities and resource levels. AIM also states that bundle guidance is not meant to dictate an exclusive course of treatment; local adaptation is appropriate, while standardization within an institution is strongly encouraged. B falsely makes the bundle inflexible across settings. C incorrectly limits systems-based safety work to patients already labeled high risk. D misuses a quality-improvement framework as a substitute for bedside assessment and individualized clinical judgment.
educational_objective: Implement maternal patient safety bundles as evidence-informed, standardized quality-improvement frameworks that are adapted to local resources while preserving individualized clinical assessment and treatment.
source_organization: Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health / American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
source_document_title: Patient Safety Bundles; Obstetric Hemorrhage Patient Safety Bundle

source_locator: AIM Patient Safety Bundles — PSBs are collections of evidence-informed best practices developed by multidisciplinary experts; goal is to improve care processes and outcomes; actionable steps can be adapted to a variety of facilities and resource levels; guidance is not meant to be prescriptive. AIM Obstetric Hemorrhage bundle — actionable steps adaptable to facility resources; standardization within an institution is strongly encouraged; bundle reflects evidence-informed/current patient-safety advances and does not dictate an exclusive course of treatment
source_claim_supported: AIM patient safety bundles provide evidence-informed, actionable practices that can be adapted to local resources and standardized within an institution; they support but do not replace individualized clinical judgment or dictate one exclusive treatment course.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing

blueprint_topic: Management of Care — implementation of maternal patient safety bundles
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source broad outcome claim into an implementation decision grounded in current AIM language. The final item tests the essential balance between evidence-informed standardization and local/patient-specific adaptation, and explicitly prevents the misconception that a safety bundle is an inflexible national order set or a replacement for clinical judgment.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: maternal patient safety / quality improvement / safety-bundle implementation
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current AIM patient-safety-bundle and obstetric-hemorrhage bundle pages. Evidence-informed best practices, actionable/adaptable steps, local resource adaptation, institutional standardization, and nonprescriptive clinical use are explicit.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses the exact implementation principles without claiming that one bundle element independently improves outcomes or that all facilities must have identical resources. The final wording preserves individual clinical judgment.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it balances evidence-informed standardization with facility and patient-specific adaptation.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; AIM explicitly allows adaptation and does not define bundles as inflexible universal order sets.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; bundles are systems-based approaches to clinically specific maternal conditions and are not restricted only to patients already labeled high risk.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; bundles guide processes and quality improvement but do not replace individualized assessment or treatment decisions.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A accurately integrates standardization, adaptability, and clinical judgment.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe plausible implementation philosophies for the same safety bundle rather than unrelated bundle content.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care is directly aligned because the construct is evidence-based systems implementation, quality improvement, and coordination of care.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked current AIM definitions, evidence-informed versus evidence-proven outcome wording, local adaptation, institutional standardization, nonprescriptive language, patient-specific judgment, high-risk-only misconception, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
